introduction.heading: What are WebSockets?
introduction.description: A WebSocket is a persistent, full-duplex connection between a browser and a server. Instead of the client asking and the server answering once per HTTP request, both sides keep a single connection open and can send messages to each other at any time. That makes WebSockets a natural fit for anything that needs to feel instant - chat apps, live dashboards, multiplayer games, and collaborative editors.

concepts.title: Full-Duplex
concepts.description: Client and server can both send messages at any time on the same open connection - no waiting your turn like request/response

concepts.title: The Handshake
concepts.description: A WebSocket connection starts life as a normal HTTP request with an Upgrade: websocket header, then switches protocols

concepts.title: Persistent Connection
concepts.description: The connection stays open until either side closes it, instead of ending after each exchange like a typical HTTP call

concepts.title: Frames
concepts.description: Messages travel as small text or binary frames, so the protocol handles chunking large payloads for you

concepts.title: wss://
concepts.description: The secure WebSocket scheme, running over TLS - use it in production the same way you'd use https:// over http://

lifecycle.heading: The Connection Lifecycle
lifecycle.description: A WebSocket moves through four states, tracked by its readyState property: CONNECTING (0) while the handshake is in flight, OPEN (1) once it succeeds and messages can flow both ways, CLOSING (2) after either side starts shutting the connection down, and CLOSED (3) once it's fully gone. Four events mirror those transitions: onopen, onmessage, onerror, and onclose.

gettingStarted.heading: Getting Started
steps: Create a socket with new WebSocket("wss://your-server/path")
Wait for socket.onopen before sending anything - the handshake isn't done until it fires
Send data with socket.send(...) - strings, JSON.stringify'd objects, or binary data all work
Handle incoming data in socket.onmessage - the payload is on event.data
Always wire up socket.onclose and socket.onerror so a dropped connection doesn't leave your UI hanging
On the server, reach for a library like ws in Node.js - browsers can open connections but can't accept them

practiceTopics.title: Sending & Receiving Messages
practiceTopics.description: Send structured JSON over the wire and see how a server-style handler responds

practiceTopics.title: Broadcasting to Multiple Clients
practiceTopics.description: Watch a server fan one message out to every connection it's holding open

practiceTopics.title: Heartbeats (Ping/Pong)
practiceTopics.description: Keep a connection alive and detect a dead one with periodic pings

practiceTopics.title: Reconnecting with Backoff
practiceTopics.description: Handle a dropped connection gracefully by retrying with increasing delays

fullExample.heading: Full Example, Step by Step
fullExample.title: A tiny chat server and client with the ws library
fullExample.description: This ties the core concepts above together in one realistic pair of files: a Node.js server that tracks connected clients and broadcasts messages, and a browser client that connects to it. Click through the steps to see which lines each one is talking about.

steps.label: Start a WebSocket server
steps.explanation: The ws package is the standard way to run a WebSocket server in Node - createServer() from http won't accept upgrade requests on its own. Passing a port has it listen directly.

steps.label: Track connected clients
steps.explanation: A Set holding every open socket is how a server knows who to broadcast to later - there's no built-in "send to everyone" method.

steps.label: React to a new connection
steps.explanation: The "connection" event fires once per client, right after the HTTP-to-WebSocket handshake succeeds, handing you that client's socket.

steps.label: Receive and parse a message
steps.explanation: Frames arrive as raw text or binary data - JSON.parse turns the string back into the object the client sent.

steps.label: Broadcast to everyone else
steps.explanation: Looping over the Set and checking readyState === OPEN avoids sending to a client mid-handshake or already closing, and skipping the sender echoes the message to everyone but them.

steps.label: Clean up on disconnect
steps.explanation: "close" fires whether the client left on purpose or the connection just dropped - removing it from the Set stops the server from trying to send to a dead socket.

steps.label: Connect from the browser
steps.explanation: new WebSocket(url) starts the handshake immediately - there's no separate .connect() call.

steps.label: Send once the handshake finishes
steps.explanation: onopen only fires after the server accepts the connection - calling send() any earlier throws an InvalidStateError because the socket isn't OPEN yet.

steps.label: Handle incoming messages
steps.explanation: onmessage fires once per frame the server sends - here that's every chat message another client broadcasts.
